title: Complete Bible School & Christian Ministry Certificate
description: One complete 10-module Bible school program from new believer to confident Christian leader and Bible teacher: foundations of the faith, Old & New Testament surveys, hermeneutics, Christian doctrine, prayer & spiritual formation, evangelism & discipleship, leadership & ministry, preaching & teaching, and a capstone ministry project with a Certificate of Completion.
outcomes: Understand the whole Bible — Old and New Testaments — and its story of redemption
Interpret Scripture faithfully using sound hermeneutics
Know core Christian doctrine (God, Christ, Spirit, salvation, church, last things)
Grow in prayer, worship and spiritual formation
Do evangelism and discipleship and lead in ministry with integrity
Prepare and deliver Bible studies and sermons, and build a ministry portfolio
about: This is the complete TIH Bible School & Christian Ministry Certificate — the three former Bible courses combined into one full ten-module program.

It follows the core subjects taught in Bible colleges worldwide: Bible surveys, interpretation, doctrine, spiritual formation, evangelism, leadership, and preaching and teaching. Every content lesson has a video and printable notes; downloadable resources include Bible study guides, sermon templates, discipleship manuals, prayer journals and ministry planning tools.

Recommended resources: The Holy Bible, a Study Bible, Bible dictionary/atlas/concordance, Blue Letter Bible and the YouVersion Bible App. A capstone ministry project builds your portfolio, and after the graduation assessment you receive a Certificate of Completion.
requirements: A Bible (any reliable translation) and a teachable heart
A notebook or device for study notes and journaling
A desire to grow as a believer and serve in ministry

faqs.question: Do I need to be a Christian to take this course?
faqs.answer: No. This course is perfect for seekers with questions as well as new believers. Come as you are and explore the faith honestly.

faqs.question: Do I need to know the Bible already?
faqs.answer: Not at all. Every lesson explains the Scriptures clearly and points you to the verses so you can read them yourself.

faqs.question: Will I get a certificate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Complete all modules and pass the final assessment (70%) to earn your TIH Bible School certificate.

lessons.html:
Module 1: Foundations of Christian FaithComplete Bible lesson

📖 Introduction to the Bible

This lesson explains Introduction to the Bible through the biblical text, its context, the whole story of Scripture, and responsible Christian practice.

Definition

The Bible is a library of writings received by Christians as Scripture, telling the unified story of God, creation, humanity, covenant, Jesus Christ, the church, and new creation.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Introduction to the Bible

The Bible is a library of writings received by Christians as Scripture, telling the unified story of God, creation, humanity, covenant, Jesus Christ, the church, and new creation.

canon

the recognized collection of writings received as Scripture by a faith community

covenant

a binding relationship established by God with promises, responsibilities, and signs

redemption

God’s work of rescue and restoration from sin and its consequences

Scripture map

Core passages: Genesis 1–3; Luke 24:25–27; 2 Timothy 3:14–17.

Read the complete paragraph or narrative around every reference. Ask who speaks, to whom, why, what happens before and after, and how the passage contributes to its book and the Bible’s wider story.

Detailed explanation

The Bible is a library of writings received by Christians as Scripture, telling the unified story of God, creation, humanity, covenant, Jesus Christ, the church, and new creation. Read each passage in its literary and historical setting, then locate it within the whole biblical story.

  • Text: observe repeated words, structure, persons, actions, commands, promises, contrasts, and connections.
  • Context: identify literary genre, historical setting, authorial purpose, audience, and place in redemptive history.
  • Theology: state what the passage reveals about God, humanity, sin, grace, covenant, Christ, church, mission, or hope.
  • Formation: move toward faithful belief and action without making the passage say more than its evidence permits.

Study method

  1. Read the text: Read the full passage slowly in more than one translation when possible and record what is actually present.
  2. Trace redemption: Investigate book setting, genre, argument, original audience, cultural background, and relevant cross-references.
  3. State the doctrine: Write the main idea in one clear sentence and explain how the evidence supports it.
  4. Live faithfully: Name a specific faithful response, a boundary against misuse, and a way to evaluate the fruit.

Worked passage study

Observation: In the listed passages, record the main actor, problem, divine initiative, human response, and stated result. Do not begin with a modern slogan.

Interpretation: Read each passage in its literary and historical setting, then locate it within the whole biblical story. The responsible conclusion must fit the sentence, surrounding section, purpose of the book, and wider biblical witness.

Application: Turn the main idea into one belief to confess, one practice to begin or correct, one person or community to serve, and one accountability check.

Common mistakes and corrections

  • Isolated verse: quoting a line without context. Correction: read the paragraph, book purpose, genre, and covenant setting.
  • Personal meaning only: asking “what it means to me” before asking what the text communicates. Correction: establish meaning, then bridge carefully to application.
  • False certainty: presenting one tradition’s disputed conclusion as the only faithful view. Correction: identify shared foundations and represent major views fairly.
  • Unhealthy application: using Scripture to control, shame, conceal harm, or claim immunity from questions. Correction: require truth, consent, love, justice, safeguarding, and accountability.

Guided practice and Model answer

Question: How should a student explain and apply Introduction to the Bible faithfully?

Model answer: I begin with Genesis 1–3; Luke 24:25–27; 2 Timothy 3:14–17 and read each reference in its complete literary setting. I identify the genre, speaker or author, first audience, purpose, and place in the Bible’s redemptive story. The central teaching is: The Bible is a library of writings received by Christians as Scripture, telling the unified story of God, creation, humanity, covenant, Jesus Christ, the church, and new creation. I then test that statement against the passage’s structure and relevant biblical texts, noting where Christian traditions differ rather than hiding the difference. A faithful application should grow from the central teaching, respect other people’s dignity and freedom, agree with the wider witness of Scripture, and produce truthful love, holiness, justice, service, and accountable practice. I will discuss the conclusion with mature leaders, correct it if the textual evidence is weak, and never use a claimed interpretation to excuse harm or avoid proper authority.

Summary

Introduction to the Bible belongs to Foundations of Christian Faith. Mastery means defining it clearly, using Scripture in context, tracing whole-Bible connections, explaining the teaching fairly, applying it concretely, and remaining humble and accountable.

Faithful and responsible practice: Where faithful Christian traditions differ, identify the main views fairly, show their biblical reasoning, and follow your church or denominational standards without misrepresenting others.

🔍 Context and Background

This lesson explains Context and Background through the biblical text, its context, the whole story of Scripture, and responsible Christian practice.

Definition

Context includes the surrounding passage, book argument, author, audience, occasion, culture, geography, and place in salvation history that constrain a text’s meaning.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Context and Background

Context includes the surrounding passage, book argument, author, audience, occasion, culture, geography, and place in salvation history that constrain a text’s meaning.

exegesis

careful explanation that draws meaning from a text in its context

genre

a recognizable kind of literature with conventions that guide reading

application

a faithful response that carries a text’s principle into the learner’s setting

Scripture map

Core passages: Jeremiah 29; 1 Corinthians 8–11; Philippians 4:10–20.

Read the complete paragraph or narrative around every reference. Ask who speaks, to whom, why, what happens before and after, and how the passage contributes to its book and the Bible’s wider story.

Detailed explanation

Context includes the surrounding passage, book argument, author, audience, occasion, culture, geography, and place in salvation history that constrain a text’s meaning. Read before and after the verse, identify the communication situation, and verify background with reliable sources.

  • Text: observe repeated words, structure, persons, actions, commands, promises, contrasts, and connections.
  • Context: identify literary genre, historical setting, authorial purpose, audience, and place in redemptive history.
  • Theology: state what the passage reveals about God, humanity, sin, grace, covenant, Christ, church, mission, or hope.
  • Formation: move toward faithful belief and action without making the passage say more than its evidence permits.

Study method

  1. Observe: Read the full passage slowly in more than one translation when possible and record what is actually present.
  2. Study context: Investigate book setting, genre, argument, original audience, cultural background, and relevant cross-references.
  3. Interpret: Write the main idea in one clear sentence and explain how the evidence supports it.
  4. Apply: Name a specific faithful response, a boundary against misuse, and a way to evaluate the fruit.

Worked passage study

Observation: In the listed passages, record the main actor, problem, divine initiative, human response, and stated result. Do not begin with a modern slogan.

Interpretation: Read before and after the verse, identify the communication situation, and verify background with reliable sources. The responsible conclusion must fit the sentence, surrounding section, purpose of the book, and wider biblical witness.

Application: Turn the main idea into one belief to confess, one practice to begin or correct, one person or community to serve, and one accountability check.

  • Isolated verse: quoting a line without context. Correction: read the paragraph, book purpose, genre, and covenant setting.

lessons.html:
Module 10: Ministry CapstoneSupervised ministry capstone

🏗️ Ministry Portfolio

A Ministry Portfolio is organized evidence of learning and service, including interpretation work, lesson plans, project records, feedback, ethics documentation, reflection, and future development goals.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Ministry Portfolio

A Ministry Portfolio is organized evidence of learning and service, including interpretation work, lesson plans, project records, feedback, ethics documentation, reflection, and future development goals.

ministry evidence

verifiable work products and records showing what was planned, delivered, and learned

rubric

published criteria used to judge the quality of a performance or project

reflection

honest analysis of decisions, results, feedback, limitations, and next steps

Biblical foundation

Read: 1 Timothy 4:12–16; 2 Timothy 2:1–2.

Remove confidential data, obtain permissions, label your own contribution, and reflect honestly on strengths and needed growth.

Project brief

Create an authentic ministry artifact for a clearly identified church or community need. Work under an accountable supervisor and separate what Scripture says, what you infer, what your tradition teaches, and what the local situation requires.

  1. Describe the audience, verified need, stakeholders, intended outcome, exclusions, and ministry authority.
  2. Provide a sound passage study and theological rationale using context, genre, and whole-Bible connections.
  3. Create a delivery plan with roles, timeline, budget, permissions, accessibility, safeguarding, confidentiality, and referral routes.
  4. Deliver or simulate the work ethically; collect consented evidence and feedback without exaggerating numbers or outcomes.
  5. Evaluate results against the rubric, document changes, and write a specific follow-up and growth plan.

Required portfolio evidence

  • Needs assessment, supervisor approval, Scripture study, plan, budget, risk and safeguarding checklist.
  • Teaching materials or service artifact, delivery record, anonymized feedback, and outcome evidence.
  • Reflection separating success, limitation, unexpected result, ethical concern, correction, and next action.

Assessment rubric

AreaEvidence of quality
Biblical faithfulnessAccurate context, main idea, whole-Bible connection, and honest use of sources.
Ministry designVerified need, clear outcome, feasible plan, community participation, and follow-up.
Ethics and safetyConsent, boundaries, safeguarding, privacy, financial integrity, reporting, and accountability.
CommunicationAudience-appropriate, clear, respectful, accessible, and free from manipulation.
EvaluationCredible evidence, honest limits, feedback, reflection, correction, and next steps.

Guided practice and Model answer

Task: Explain what makes this capstone ready for responsible ministry use.

Model answer: The work begins with a real need confirmed by the people affected, accountable church authorization, and a clear outcome. Its biblical foundation comes from passages read in context rather than isolated slogans. The plan names roles, costs, permissions, safeguarding controls, confidentiality limits, referral routes, and a stop or escalation process. Delivery respects freedom and never uses aid, authority, fear, or spiritual claims to pressure anyone. Evidence is accurate and anonymized, feedback includes critical voices, and the reflection states both fruit and failure. A supervisor reviews the work, corrections are recorded, and follow-up is realistic. If safety, truthfulness, consent, or accountability cannot be secured, the project must pause or change.

Faithful and responsible practice: Where faithful Christian traditions differ, identify the main views fairly, show their biblical reasoning, and follow your church or denominational standards without misrepresenting others. Ministry must use consent, safeguarding, confidentiality, transparent finances, role boundaries, reporting procedures, and referral to qualified authorities or professionals when needed.

Further study

  • BibleProject study guides
  • Yale Bible Study resources
  • Lausanne Movement mission resources

Read the listed Bible passages in a trusted translation. Compare translations when wording affects interpretation, and consult reliable study Bibles, commentaries, maps, and your church’s confession or teaching standards.
